title: Disability & the Politics of Help
hook: Grabbing a wheelchair or a blind man's arm feels like kindness, and to the person on the receiving end it often feels like being moved like furniture.
why:
Most people who have not lived with disability have never been taught how to behave around it, and many of them feel it. In a 2014 survey for the disability charity Scope, about two-thirds of British adults said they felt uncomfortable talking to disabled people, most often because they were afraid of saying or doing the wrong thing. That discomfort shows in the body. People stare, or look carefully away. They talk to the companion instead. They lean on the wheelchair, grab an arm, or rush in to help with something the person was managing perfectly well.

For a disabled man, these small moments add up. Each one says, in the language of the body, that he is less capable than he is, or that his body and his equipment are open to anyone. For the man doing the helping, they are usually well meant, and that is exactly why they persist.

This chapter covers the politics of help: asking before acting, meeting someone at eye level, guiding a blind person properly, reading a face that cannot move, the conventions of Deaf space, the trap of assuming that one difference means many, and reading a different body against its own baseline.

teach.p:
The most common mistake non-disabled people make around disability is not hostility but help. In 2019 the psychologist Michelle Nario-Redmond and her colleagues described three forms of prejudice against disabled people. Hostile ableism includes bullying and abuse. Benevolent ableism treats disabled people as fragile, childlike or in need of rescue. Ambivalent ableism mixes the two. In accounts of what disabled people meet day to day, help that nobody asked for is among the experiences most often reported.

Unasked-for help is a nonverbal act. Someone takes hold of a wheelchair and starts pushing. Someone grabs the elbow of a blind man at a crossing and steers him across. Someone lifts a bag from a man walking with a cane. Each says, without words, that the helper has judged the situation and decided that the other person cannot manage it. It also takes away control: the person being helped may have been going somewhere else, at a different pace, by a different route.

The rule disability organisations teach is simple. Ask first: would you like a hand? Then wait for the answer, and accept it if it is no. If it is yes, ask how. A wheelchair user may want the door held but not the chair pushed. A blind man may want directions rather than an arm.

The figure here sits upright in a manual wheelchair, hands resting near the rims. The chair is how he moves, and he is in control of it. Treat it as part of his personal space, as you would treat his body: do not lean on it, hang a bag on it, or move it without asking.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if disabled people generally welcomed help given without asking. Accounts gathered by disability researchers and organisations consistently list unasked-for help among the most common and least welcome experiences.
teach.pullQuote: Ask first, then wait for the answer, and accept it if it is no.

teach.p:
A seated person's eyes are around 120 centimetres from the floor; a standing man's are typically 40 to 50 centimetres higher. In a passing exchange this hardly matters. In a longer conversation, standing close to someone in a wheelchair forces him to tip his head back and look up, which tires the neck, and it puts him in a position this book has described many times as lower status: looked down on, literally.

The fix is easy. For anything longer than a passing word, sit down if there is a chair, or step back far enough that the other person can see your face without craning. Crouching can work for a moment, but it can look like talking to a child, so a chair is usually better.

A second rule matters as much: talk to the person, not the companion. The habit of addressing a disabled person's partner, carer or friend instead of the disabled person himself is so common that a long-running BBC Radio 4 programme on disability took its name from it: Does He Take Sugar? Waiters ask the companion what he will order. Receptionists ask the companion to fill in his form. Direct your eyes, your questions and your body to the person himself, even if he uses an interpreter or a communication aid.

The figures here sit at the same height, facing each other. The standing man has pulled up a chair. Nothing about the conversation needs to change except the height of his eyes, and that one change turns it into a conversation between equals.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if height made no difference to how a conversation feels. Wheelchair users widely report that being stood over, and being bypassed in favour of a companion, are among the most diminishing parts of everyday encounters.

teach.p:
A long white cane tells others that its user is blind or has low vision. It does not tell them he needs help, and it is never an invitation to take his arm. Being grabbed and steered is disorienting: the blind person loses his own sense of where he is, may be pulled off his route, and may have no idea who has hold of him.

The technique taught by sight loss charities such as the RNIB is called sighted guiding. First, introduce yourself and ask whether he would like help. If he would, offer your elbow rather than taking his. He holds your arm just above the elbow and walks half a step behind, which lets him feel through your arm when you turn, stop, step up or step down. Walk at his pace, and say what is coming: a kerb, steps going up, a narrow doorway. For a narrow gap, move your guiding arm behind your back to signal that he should step in behind you.

A few other habits help. Say your name when you approach, since he may not recognise your voice. Say when you are leaving, so that he is not left talking to empty air. Do not pet, feed or distract a guide dog in harness; it is working. And give directions in words that do not depend on sight: about ten steps ahead, on your left, rather than over there.

The figure here walks with his cane sweeping ahead, head level, his free arm relaxed. He is not lost. He is travelling the way he has learned to travel, and the most useful thing a stranger can do is keep out of the cane's path, or ask.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if grabbing a blind person's arm were as effective and welcome as offering an elbow. Sight loss charities teach the offered elbow precisely because it leaves the blind person in control and lets him read movement through your arm.

teach.p:
Much of this book has been about reading faces. Some faces cannot be read in the usual way. Facial paralysis can follow a stroke, Bell's palsy, surgery or injury, and some people are born with it, as in Moebius syndrome, a rare condition that leaves the face largely unable to move. A man with Moebius syndrome may feel delight, amusement or grief as fully as anyone, but none of it reaches the muscles that smile or frown.

The psychologist Kathleen Bogart, who herself has Moebius syndrome, has studied how others respond. In a 2014 study with Linda Tickle-Degnen and Nalini Ambady, observers watched or listened to people with facial paralysis describing happy and sad experiences. People with more severe paralysis were rated as less happy than people with milder paralysis, whichever combination of face, voice and body the observers were given. The still face was read as a flat mood.

Bogart's work also points to a remedy. People with facial paralysis, especially those born with it, often express emotion through other channels: the voice, gesture, posture, the timing of laughter. In 2015 Bogart and Tickle-Degnen reported that a brief training, which encouraged observers to attend to those channels rather than the face, improved their impressions. The lesson reaches beyond paralysis. When a face is still, because of a condition, medication, a culture of restraint or simple temperament, listen to the voice and watch the hands before deciding what someone feels.

The figure here stands with a neutral face and a level gaze. Without his voice and the context, nothing in that face tells you whether he is content, bored or moved, and that is the point: a still face is the absence of a signal, not a signal of absence.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if observers read the emotions of people with facial paralysis as accurately as anyone else's. Bogart and colleagues found that severe paralysis led observers to see less happiness than the speakers were describing.
teach.pullQuote: A still face is the absence of a signal, not a signal of absence.

teach.p:
Deaf people who use a sign language, such as British Sign Language or American Sign Language, share a culture with its own nonverbal conventions, and several of them reverse hearing habits. Many write Deaf with a capital D to mark that cultural identity, as distinct from the medical fact of hearing loss.

Getting attention is the first difference. Calling a name across the room does nothing. Instead, Deaf people wave within the other person's line of sight, tap a shoulder or arm lightly, stamp on a wooden floor so that the vibration carries, or flick the lights to get a group's attention. To a hearing person, a tap on the shoulder from a near stranger can feel intrusive; in Deaf company it is ordinary manners.

Eye contact is the second. A signed conversation is visual, so the person watching must keep looking. Looking away while someone signs is like covering your ears while they speak, and it can end the conversation. Hearing people raised to soften their gaze may find the steadiness intense; it is simply how the language works.

The third is the face. In sign languages, facial expressions do grammatical work: raised eyebrows can mark a yes-or-no question, furrowed brows a question asking who, what or where, and mouth shapes can change what a sign means. An expressive face on a Deaf signer is often grammar, not emotion, and reading it as anger or drama is a mistake.

For someone who lip-reads, face him, keep your hands and food away from your mouth, do not shout or exaggerate, and stand where the light falls on your face. Only part of speech is visible on the lips, so lip-reading is tiring and partial. The figure here waves, which in Deaf company is the polite way to say: I would like to talk to you.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if Deaf signers used attention-getting, eye contact and facial expression in the same way hearing speakers do. Sign language research and Deaf community guidance describe them as different, and in some respects opposite.

teach.p:
In her 1960 book Physical Disability: A Psychological Approach, the psychologist Beatrice Wright described a pattern she called spread: the tendency to assume that a disability in one area affects many others. Spread is why people raise their voices to a blind man, as if he were also deaf. It is why they speak slowly and simply to a wheelchair user, as if his legs and his mind were connected. It is why a man with a speech impairment is assumed to have an intellectual one.

Spread also works through the body. A slow, careful gait, a cane, a tremor or a stiff posture can be read as weakness of mind or mood, when it says nothing about either. A man who walks with a cane after a hip operation is the same man he was before it. The figure here walks with a cane, head up, at his own pace. Nothing about the pace of his feet tells you the pace of his thinking.

Not every disability is visible. Many people live with chronic pain, fatigue, epilepsy, heart conditions, mental illness or hearing loss that nobody can see. A man who takes the lift for one floor, sits in a priority seat or leaves a party early may be managing something invisible. In the United Kingdom and increasingly elsewhere, a lanyard printed with sunflowers, introduced at Gatwick Airport in 2016, is recognised as a discreet signal that the wearer has a hidden disability and may need extra time, space or help.

The working rule is to assume nothing beyond what you know. A disability tells you about one thing. Let the person tell you about everything else.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if a visible disability reliably predicted other impairments. Spread, as Wright described it, is an error of perception, and disabled people report meeting it constantly: being shouted at, talked down to and spoken about in the third person.

teach.p:
Earlier chapters have stressed reading against a baseline: noticing change in a person rather than comparing him with a general norm. Disability makes this rule essential. A man with Parkinson's disease may have a tremor, a soft voice and a face that moves less than it did, none of which signals nerves or lack of interest. A man with cerebral palsy may have movements that look tense or abrupt. A man recovering from a brain injury may speak slowly or flatly. Someone with a chronic pain condition may shift, wince or stand up often, which is not impatience.

Read each of these against the person's own pattern. Once you know how someone usually moves and sounds, changes become meaningful again: a man whose tremor is worse than usual may be tired, stressed or unwell, and a wheelchair user who has stopped joining in may be shut out by the layout of the room rather than uninterested.

Asking is allowed. Disabled people differ in how much they want to talk about their bodies, but most prefer a direct, respectful question to silent guessing or staring. Is there anything that would make this easier? is usually welcome. Questions from strangers about how someone became disabled usually are not.

Finally, notice the room. Much of what looks like a person's limitation is a limitation of the space: steps, narrow aisles, loud rooms, dim light, tables at the wrong height. The figure here listens, leaning slightly forward, his attention on the other person, the posture of someone trying to learn how this particular person works rather than assuming.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the usual cues of emotion and attention applied unchanged to people with different bodies. Tremor, reduced facial movement and unusual movement are features of many conditions, and say nothing by themselves about mood or interest.

poseGallery.annotation: For a conversation of more than a minute, sit down or step back. He should not have to crane to see your face.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Moving in to help without asking
poseGallery.annotation: Unasked-for help takes away control. Ask whether he would like a hand, and accept no as an answer.
In a signed conversation, looking away is like covering your ears. Keep your eyes on the signer.

caseStudy:
Ravi, thirty-nine, became a wheelchair user after a cycling accident three years ago. He works as an engineer, plays wheelchair basketball on Thursdays and has a dry sense of humour about most things. What wears him down, he says, is not the chair but the way people behave around it.

Strangers take hold of his handles to push him up ramps he was managing. Waiters ask his wife what he would like. At work events, colleagues stand in a tight circle above him, and he spends the evening looking at belt buckles or straining his neck until he gives up and leaves early. Once, in a shop, a man patted him on the shoulder and told him he was an inspiration for being out.

His brother-in-law, Paul, a kind man who had never known anyone disabled, admitted that he had done several of these things in the first year. At a family wedding he had pushed Ravi across the lawn without asking, because the grass looked difficult, and had been hurt when Ravi snapped at him. Ravi's sister explained it later: it was like someone grabbing your arm and steering you across a room.

Paul changed a few habits. He asks before he helps, and when Ravi says no, he leaves it. At family gatherings he pulls up a chair rather than standing over him, and he has noticed that others start sitting down too. When a waiter turned to him to ask what Ravi wanted, he simply looked at Ravi and waited.

Ravi says the difference is not that Paul is careful around him now. It is that Paul has stopped being careful around him, and started treating him as the same man he was before, who happens to sit down.
observe: Notice, the next time you see a wheelchair user in conversation, the heights of everyone's eyes and who is looking up.
Notice whom staff address when a disabled person is with a companion: the person, or the companion.
Notice any impulse you have to help a disabled stranger, and whether you would ask first.
Notice a space you use every day, such as your office or a favourite café, and where steps, narrow gaps, noise or lighting would make it hard to use.

drills.name: Ask, Wait, Accept
steps: Think of three situations where you might offer help to a disabled person: a door, a ramp, a crossing.
For each, write the words you would use to offer help.
Write what you will do if the answer is no.
Practise saying the offer aloud until it sounds natural rather than anxious.

drills.name: Learn Sighted Guiding
steps: Watch a demonstration of sighted guiding from a sight loss charity.
With a willing friend, practise offering your elbow while he walks with his eyes closed.
Walk a short route that includes a doorway, a step and a narrow gap.
Swap roles, and notice what it feels like to be guided well, and to be pulled.
Note one thing you would do differently with a stranger.

drills.name: Eye-Level Audit
steps: At your next meeting or social event, notice who is sitting and who is standing.
Sit down for one conversation with a seated person you would normally stand over.
Notice how the conversation changes in length and tone.

drills.name: Spread Check
steps: Think of a disabled person you know or have met.
List any assumptions you made about him beyond what his disability actually involves.
Ask what evidence you had for each one.
Write one sentence about what you will assume next time, which is nothing extra.

quiz.q: A colleague says that when you see a wheelchair user on a ramp, the kind thing is to start pushing, since he can always say if he minds. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, since most wheelchair users welcome a push and will say so if they mind it
Ask first and wait for an answer, since unasked-for help takes away the person's control
Never offer help at all, since any offer of help is an insult to a disabled person
Push only on the steepest ramps, since gentle ramps are easy enough for anyone to manage
quiz.explain: Unasked-for help is among the experiences disabled people most often report as unwelcome. Asking first, and accepting no, leaves the person in control of his own body and chair.

quiz.q: What did Bogart, Tickle-Degnen and Ambady find in their 2014 study of facial paralysis?
options: People with severe paralysis were rated as less happy than people with milder paralysis
Observers read the emotions of people with paralysis as accurately as anyone else's
Observers relied on the face alone and ignored the voice and body completely in every case
People with facial paralysis were rated as happier than others, because they seemed calm
quiz.explain: Observers rated people with severe paralysis as less happy, whichever combination of face, voice and body they were given. A still face was read as a flat mood.

quiz.q: In a conversation in sign language, what does looking away from the signer usually do?
options: It shows respect, as it does in the many hearing cultures that soften their eye contact
It has no effect at all, since the signer will simply carry on until you look back again
It is like covering your ears while someone speaks, and it can end the conversation
It signals that you have understood the point and are ready for the signer to move on
quiz.explain: A signed conversation is visual, so the person watching has to keep looking. Breaking eye contact cuts off the language itself, not just a social signal.

quiz.q: What did Beatrice Wright mean by spread?
options: The way a disability gradually spreads to other parts of the body as time goes on
The tendency to assume that a disability in one area affects many others as well
The spread of disability rights laws from one country to many others since the 1990s
The way that disabled people spread their weight differently in order to stay balanced
quiz.explain: Spread is the error of assuming that one disability implies others, such as shouting at a blind man or talking down to a wheelchair user. It is a mistake in the perceiver, not a feature of the disability.

quiz.q: A blind man with a long cane is standing at a busy crossing. What fits this chapter best?
options: Take his arm firmly and walk him across, since the traffic is fast and dangerous
Say nothing at all, since offering help to a blind man is always unwelcome to him
Call out directions to him from across the street as soon as the lights change
Introduce yourself, ask if he would like help, and offer your elbow if he would
quiz.explain: Sighted guiding starts with an introduction and a question. If he accepts, offering your elbow lets him hold on and feel your movements, leaving him in control.

quiz.q: At a work event, a waiter asks you what your colleague, who uses a wheelchair, would like to drink. What fits this chapter best?
options: Answer for him, since you know what he usually drinks and it saves everyone some time
Look at your colleague and wait, so that the waiter turns to him and asks him directly
Tell the waiter off loudly, so that everyone can see how rude he was to your colleague
Go and fetch the drink yourself, so that nobody else has to deal with the situation
quiz.explain: Talking to the companion instead of the disabled person is so common that a BBC programme on disability was named after it. Turning your eyes to him redirects the waiter without embarrassing anyone.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific encounter with a disabled person, as a stranger, colleague, friend or relative, or a time when you were treated differently because of a disability or injury of your own. Describe what bodies did: who stood and who sat, who was addressed, who helped, and whether anyone asked first. What did the person on the receiving end seem to feel? If you could replay the moment, what would you do differently with your eyes, your hands or your position in the room?
reflection.guidance: Many people feel embarrassed recalling these moments, since most of the mistakes were made with good intentions. That is the point of the exercise. Focus on concrete behaviour, such as height, gaze and touch, rather than on whether you were a good person, and include any time you were on the receiving end, even with a temporary injury.

failureMode: The first failure is to help without asking, taking hold of a chair, an arm or a bag, which removes the other person's control however kindly it is meant. The second is to stand over a seated person through a long conversation, or to address the companion instead of the person. The third is to grab a blind man rather than offer an elbow, or to walk away without saying so. The fourth is to read a still face as a still mood, when paralysis, medication or temperament may hide what someone feels. The fifth is to bring hearing habits into Deaf space: calling out, looking away while someone signs, reading grammatical expressions as emotion. And the sixth is spread: assuming that a disability in one area means others, and talking down to a man whose mind is untouched.
